the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad (N=99,645), aggregating all encounters between a given player and referee over the season
99,645 player-referee dyads were analyzed
there were 1,214 unique players (236 dark-skinned, 978 light-skinned)
there were 2,768 unique referees
1,241 red card events were observed (1.25% overall rate)
light-skinned dyads numbered 83,655 (84.0%)
dark-skinned dyads numbered 15,990 (16.0%)
skin tone was rated independently by two trained coders on a 5-point scale from player profile photos
inter-rater reliability for skin tone ratings was excellent (r=0.923, 76.8% exact agreement)
the two raters' skin-tone ratings were averaged and normalized to a 0-1 scale
light skin was defined as an average rating ≤0.25
dark skin was defined as an average rating ≥0.75
medium skin tones (0.25<rating<0.75) were excluded to create clear contrast groups
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for receiving any red card (direct or yellow-red) from that referee across all encounters
log-transformed number of games was included as a covariate to control for exposure/opportunity
player position (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, forward; goalkeeper as reference) was included as a covariate
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain; England as reference) was included as a covariate
standardized player height was included as a covariate
standardized player weight was included as a covariate
height and weight were standardized (mean=0, SD=1) to improve model convergence and interpretability
the correlation between height and weight was 0.79, indicating multicollinearity was not a major concern
the original dataset contained 146,028 player-referee dyads before exclusions
21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no photo), leaving 124,621
17,015 dyads with medium skin tones were excluded, leaving 107,606
7,961 dyads were excluded for missing covariate data, leaving 99,645 dyads (68.2% of original) in the final analysis
complete case analysis was used
unshown sensitivity checks indicate missingness is not strongly related to the outcome, suggesting minimal selection bias
a natural log transformation was applied to number of games to linearize its relationship with log-odds of a red card and reduce outlier influence
height and weight were z-score standardized (mean-centered, divided by SD)
skin tone was already on a 0-1 scale from averaging the two raters' normalized scores
the primary estimation approach was logistic regression combined with g-computation (marginal standardization)
a logistic regression model was fitted predicting any red card from the dark-skin indicator, log(games), position, league, height z-score, and weight z-score

g-computation was used to estimate the adjusted risk difference by predicting P(red card) under dark_skin=1 and dark_skin=0 for all observations, averaging each to get marginal risks, and computing Risk_dark minus Risk_light

95% CIs and p-values were computed via a parametric bootstrap with 5,000 simulations drawing parameter vectors from a multivariate normal based on model coefficients/covariance, computing the risk difference per draw, using 2.5th/97.5th percentiles for the CI, and a two-sided p-value from a Normal distribution using the bootstrap SE
the secondary estimand (odds ratio) was obtained directly from the logistic regression coefficient for dark_skin, with a Wald-based 95% CI and p-value
the parametric bootstrap approach accounts for uncertainty in all model parameters
clustered standard errors or mixed-effects models were not used, despite the nested data structure (multiple dyads per player and per referee)
the primary source of dependence is through player and referee characteristics, which are already captured by the covariates and partially by league country
the parametric bootstrap from the model covariance matrix provides valid inference under the assumed model structure
a sensitivity analysis with player-clustered standard errors yielded nearly identical p-values to the primary analysis (0.024 vs. 0.023)
inter-rater reliability was high (r=0.92), suggesting minimal measurement error
